prompt: Why does a line added to a prompt's instructions cost money on every call rather than once?
hint: Think about what is sent with each message.

choices.text: The whole prompt is sent again with each message
choices.why: Right: forty messages, forty copies of the instructions.

choices.text: The provider retrains the model on the prompt each day and bills for the training
choices.why: Nothing is trained; the prompt is read on each call.

choices.text: Providers bill a fee per line
choices.why: The lab bills tokens, not lines.

choices.text: The reply repeats it
choices.why: The reply is output; the extra line is input.

prompt: `pl tokens` counts `v2-json.txt` at 69 tokens and `v2-long.txt` at 167. How many extra tokens of instructions does each call with the long prompt carry?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: A million calls cost 83,355 cents with the short prompt and 117,030 with the long one. Roughly how many percent more does the long one cost? Answer to the nearest whole number.
hint: Divide the long by the short.

prompt: Over the forty calls, did the long prompt add more input tokens or more output tokens than the short one?
hint: Compare 3,139 with 7,059, and 1,595 with 1,709.

choices.text: Input, by far
choices.why: Right: 3,920 more input tokens against 114 more output.

choices.text: Output, because the model writes longer summaries
choices.why: The summaries did grow, but by 114 tokens over forty calls.

choices.text: The same amount of each
choices.why: 3,920 against 114 is not the same.

choices.text: Neither; the totals were identical
choices.why: `pl cost` shows different totals for both.

prompt: Line 4 of `v2-long.txt` asks for a brief summary and line 16 asks for full detail. Which one does the stand-in obey?
hint: Its opening comment states the rule.

choices.text: Whichever is in capital letters, since the stand-in ranks shouting above everything else
choices.why: Neither line is in capitals, and the stand-in has no such rule.

choices.text: Neither: it averages them into a medium summary
choices.why: It picks one; it does not blend them.

choices.text: The one written last, line 16
choices.why: Right: between brief and thorough, the last one wins.

choices.text: Line 4, the first
choices.why: Order matters, but the other way round.

prompt: What happened to the summary of `t17` under the long prompt?
hint: Compare the two `pl show` outputs.

choices.text: It became the whole message, both sentences, moved into the third person
choices.why: Right: full detail won, so the summary is the message.

choices.text: It was cut to five words
choices.why: Nothing in either prompt sets a word limit.

choices.text: It disappeared from the JSON
choices.why: All three fields were there.

choices.text: It stayed one sentence
choices.why: That is what the short prompt produced.

prompt: What does the lesson say about which of two conflicting instructions a real model follows?
hint: It is offered as a practitioner's observation, not a rate.

choices.text: The first one, as the vendors' guides document
choices.why: The guides recommend clarity; they document no such rule.

choices.text: The later one, as in the stand-in, because every model reads from the top down and keeps the last word it saw
choices.why: That is the stand-in's written rule, not a property of real models.

choices.text: It depends on the model, the wording and where each sits, and shifts between versions
choices.why: Right, which is why a contradiction leaves the choice to the model.

choices.text: Whichever is in capitals
choices.why: The lesson makes no such claim.

prompt: Between an instruction to be brief and one to be thorough, the stand-in obeys the one written ___.
hint: Line 16 beat line 4.

prompt: You find two instructions in a prompt that disagree. What does the lesson recommend?
hint: Not a third line.

choices.text: Add a third line saying which of the two wins
choices.why: That leaves both in place, and the reader still has to work out which applies.

choices.text: Put the one you prefer in capitals so the model notices it
choices.why: Capitals rank rules without settling the disagreement.

choices.text: Move the preferred one to the end of the prompt and keep both
choices.why: That relies on the stand-in's rule, which real models do not share.

choices.text: Decide, and delete one
choices.why: Right: one instruction per decision.

prompt: `pl lint` prints `nothing found` for a prompt. What do you know?
hint: It is a set of word lists.

choices.text: The prompt has no contradictions, repeats or shouting of any kind
choices.why: A contradiction in other words passes it, as the `printf` example showed.

choices.text: The prompt is clear
choices.why: The linter cannot judge clarity.

choices.text: No pattern on its lists matched
choices.why: Right, and that is all it means.

choices.text: The model will follow every rule the prompt contains
choices.why: The linter never calls a model.

prompt: Why did the linter count line 13, which opens with *Never include the customer's name*, as a line that shouts?
hint: Look at how the pattern treats upper and lower case.

choices.text: Its pattern ignores case, so an ordinary capitalised word at the start of a sentence matched
choices.why: Right: a false positive, and a reason to read findings as lines to look at.

choices.text: Line 13 is written in capitals
choices.why: Only its first letter is.

choices.text: It repeats line 11
choices.why: Line 14 repeats line 11.

choices.text: It contradicts line 4
choices.why: The contradiction is between lines 4 and 16.

prompt: Which of these would `pl lint` report? Choose all that apply.
hint: It reads words, not meaning.

choices.text: The same instruction pasted on two lines
choices.why: Yes: `repeats line N`.

choices.text: IMPORTANT at the start of two lines
choices.why: Yes: two lines shouting is enough.

choices.text: *brief* in one line and *in full detail* in another
choices.why: Yes: both are on its lists.

choices.text: *Keep it to one line* and *leave nothing out*
choices.why: They disagree, but neither phrase is on its lists.

prompt: Why is a linter that misses contradictions written in other words still worth running?
hint: What kind of mistake creeps in unnoticed?

choices.text: It catches the slips that creep in on each edit, like a pasted repeat or a hurried capital
choices.why: Right: cheap, and run every time.

choices.text: It proves the prompt is correct before a model sees it
choices.why: It proves nothing of the kind; it matches patterns.

choices.text: It replaces the test set
choices.why: It never looks at a reply.

choices.text: Because the model reads the linter's output and adjusts its answers to it before replying to the customer
choices.why: The model never sees the linter's output.

prompt: After the cut, `pl compare --answers` printed `same answer 40, different answer 0`. What does that tell you?
hint: It compares one field, read without the wrapping.

choices.text: The cut prompt passes all forty messages on every check, wrapping included
choices.why: It passed 24 of 40; `--answers` ignores the wrapping.

choices.text: The forty replies are byte for byte the replies the long prompt gave
choices.why: The summaries and the wrapping differ.

choices.text: The sign test found the difference significant
choices.why: The sign test gave p = 0.359.

choices.text: Every category stayed the same
choices.why: Right: the content of the answers did not move.

prompt: The short prompt passed 24 of 40 and the long one 19, with `p = 0.359` on the 19 that changed. What is the right reading?
hint: How often does chance produce a split like that?

choices.text: A split this uneven turns up about one time in three by chance, so the move is noise
choices.why: Right: the cut lost nothing and did not win either.

choices.text: The short prompt is better
choices.why: The count went up, but not by more than chance would.

choices.text: The long prompt is better
choices.why: It passed fewer.

choices.text: The test set is broken
choices.why: Nothing points to that.

prompt: Why can `cases/dev.jsonl` not tell you whether dropping the rule about customers' names was safe?
hint: What would a case have to contain?

choices.text: The harness strips names out before the call is made
choices.why: The harness sends the message as it is.

choices.text: The stand-in cannot read names because it only looks at its keyword lists
choices.why: Even so, a name in the message would reach the summary.

choices.text: None of its messages has a name in it
choices.why: Right: the count is the same with the rule or without it.

choices.text: It is too small
choices.why: Size is not the problem; coverage is.

prompt: How many tokens per call did cutting `v2-long.txt` down to `v2-json.txt` save?
hint: Input per call was 176.5 and became 78.5.

prompt: `t08` passed under the long prompt and failed under the short one. Why?
hint: Look at what came before the JSON.

choices.text: The long prompt's rule against extra fields also told the model to drop any sentence before the JSON
choices.why: That rule is about fields, and the stand-in has no such reading of it.

choices.text: A sentence landed before its JSON, and in the stand-in an edit reshuffles which replies get a habit
choices.why: Right: noise, not a property of the shorter prompt.

choices.text: The short prompt picked the wrong category
choices.why: The category was returns in both.

choices.text: `t08` is not in the test set
choices.why: It is one of the forty.

prompt: Put the steps of cutting a prompt safely in order.
hint: Measure last.
items: Find the decision each line makes
Keep one instruction per decision and delete repeats
Run both prompts over the same test set

prompt: Match each `pl lint` finding to what it means.
hint: One meaning each.

pairs.right: A line asking for brevity and another asking for detail
The same instruction twice, word for word
Capital words ranking some rules above the rest

right_distractors: A rule the test set never exercises

prompt: Summaries under `v2-long.txt` are too long, and a colleague wants to add `IMPORTANT: keep the summary under 10 words` at the bottom. What do you do?
hint: Where does the length problem come from?

choices.text: Add it; capitals make the model take it seriously
choices.why: Capitals add shouting and leave line 16 in place.

choices.text: Add it at the top, so it is read first and beats line 16
choices.why: In the stand-in the last instruction wins, and a third line about length leaves the conflict standing.

choices.text: Add it twice so the model cannot miss it
choices.why: A repeat is one of the linter's findings, not a fix.

choices.text: Delete line 16, then measure
choices.why: Right: remove the cause and count the effect.
